blocks.text: You are reading Google reviews for a Finnish car repair shop (autohuolto). Almost every single review — good or bad — is built from one tiny recurring skeleton: an adjective plus the word palvelu, 'service'. Once you own this one template, you can already read (and write) the opening line of nearly every review in the whole set. This is where we start.

blocks.title: Why reviews sound so similar
blocks.text: Finnish online reviews are famously short and formulaic — Finns dislike over-explaining. A five-word review like 'Hyvä palvelu, suosittelen' is completely normal and not seen as lazy. Learning this register means learning to say a lot with very little, which is very on-brand for Finnish culture in general.
Piece 1 — Palvelu: the word every review needs

blocks.content: {Palvelu|word|noun|service} is the single most common word in this whole review corpus — it shows up over 50 times. It is a neuter-feeling noun (Finnish has no grammatical gender) meaning 'service' in the customer-service sense. You will see it in two shapes: palvelu (the plain form, used as a subject: 'the service is...') and {palvelua|grammar|partitive|some service} (the partitive form, used as an object, e.g. after 'sain' — 'I got').

items.fi: Loistavaa {palvelua|grammar|partitive|service} ja käynnistä jäi hyvä mieli.
items.en: Great service, and the visit left a good feeling.

blocks.title: Just swap the adjective
blocks.text: Once you know palvelu, the whole review-writing skill becomes: pick one adjective and put it in front. Finnish adjectives usually come before the noun, exactly like English. Change the adjective, the meaning of the whole review changes — no new grammar needed yet.

blocks.content: {Suosittelen|grammar|verb, 1st person|I recommend} comes from the verb suositella, 'to recommend'. The ending -n marks 'I' — Finnish verbs carry the subject inside the verb itself, so you often don't even need a separate word for 'I'. Reviewers use this word constantly to close out a positive review, almost like a verbal stamp of approval.

blocks.title: Paul Noble Rule
blocks.text: Don't try to memorise suosittelen as a random word. Notice the -n at the end — that's 'I' baked into the verb. You'll see this same -n ending come back on other 'I' verbs later (aion — I intend to, en — I don't). Recognise the pattern, not just the word.

blocks.title: En — the negation word
blocks.text: En means 'I don't / I won't'. It sits in front of the verb, and the main verb loses its own ending: suosittelen becomes en suosittele. This tiny word flips an entire glowing review into a warning — you'll see 'En suosittele' open several negative reviews in this corpus.

lines.speaker: A
lines.en: What was the service like at the car repair shop?

lines.speaker: B
lines.en: Yes, strong recommendation. I recommend it!

blocks.title: Free word from the dialogue
blocks.text: Kyllä means 'yes' — the formal, textbook yes. You'll meet its casual cousin joo in a later lesson. For now, kyllä is exactly what you'll see written in reviews and formal speech.

blocks.content: Palvelu: PAL-ve-lu (stress always on the first syllable in Finnish, every single word). Suosittelen: SUO-sit-te-len (four even syllables, the 'uo' glides like the 'wo' in 'won't'). Ystävällinen: YS-tä-väl-li-nen (long word, but every syllable is short and even — don't swallow the ending).

blocks.title: What you now own
items: palvelu — service (the most common word in every review)
hyvä palvelu — good service (swap in erinomainen, ammattimainen, asiantunteva, huono)
en suosittele — I do not recommend (en flips the meaning)
You can now read and write the opening and closing line of almost any Finnish car-repair review
You understand why the -n ending on suosittelen carries the word 'I' inside it
